query: For high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what testable methodological hypothesis could enable improved combinations of strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance? Explain why it should work, what measurable improvement is expected relative to the state of the art, the conditions under which it should or should not hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experimental result that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Lowering the VEC in Nb‐Mo‐Ta‐V‐W high‐entropy alloys from an equimolar composition to Nb15Mo2.5Ta40V40W2.5 will enhance ductility through increased dislocation mobility (via a reduced Peierls–Nabarro barrier) while preserving high modulus and strength, yielding an alloy with improved work hardening and fracture resistance compared to the equimolar baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar NbMoTaVW, which is known to have a single-phase BCC structure, high strength but brittle room-temperature behavior (approximately 2% compressive fracture strain) and a measured yield strength around 1246 MPa.
generation.intervention: Computational screening across 38,326 compositions by varying elemental concentrations (2.5 to 40 at.%), followed by selection of Nb15Mo2.5Ta40V40W2.5 based on its low VEC and relatively high predicted Young’s modulus. This composition is then prepared via arc melting under argon.
generation.conditions: Testing is performed on as-cast specimens under room-temperature quasi-static uniaxial compression (strain rate ~5 × 10^-4 s^-1) with detailed microstructural characterization via XRD, SEM/BSE, and measurements including Vickers hardness and nanoindentation.
generation.structural_mediator: The resulting alloy maintains a single-phase BCC structure with a dendritic microstructure (approximately 240 μm grain size), providing the structural context in which the reduced VEC promotes intrinsic shear instability and delayed brittle cracking.
generation.mechanism: Reducing the VEC reduces the Peierls–Nabarro barrier, thereby promoting dislocation mobility and facilitating slip. This enhanced dislocation activity delays the onset of brittle fracture and supports work hardening, while the retention of a relatively high elastic modulus ensures that inherent strength is maintained.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to equimolar NbMoTaVW, the Nb15Mo2.5Ta40V40W2.5 alloy is expected to exhibit significantly improved ductility (substantially higher compressive fracture strain than ~2%) with only a modest reduction in yield strength and elastic modulus, and a lower density.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the as-cast, equimolar NbMoTaVW alloy with its documented properties (approximately 1246 MPa compressive yield strength, ~2% compressive fracture strain, limited plasticity, and literature-supported elastic moduli).
generation.boundary: These improvements are expected only in the as-cast state of the Nb‐Mo‐Ta‐V‐W refractory alloys under room-temperature, quasi-static compression. The predictions do not account for changes arising from different processing histories, grain refinement, secondary phase formations, or other microstructural modifications.
generation.uncertainty: There is inherent uncertainty in how microstructural factors not captured in the composition-to-modulus model (such as grain size distribution, processing-induced defects, and phase stability under different thermal treatments) might affect the actual mechanical properties. Additionally, the exact magnitude of ductility enhancement is subject to experimental variability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare both the equimolar NbMoTaVW alloy and the Nb15Mo2.5Ta40V40W2.5 alloy using identical arc melting procedures. Subject multiple specimens of each composition to room-temperature quasi-static uniaxial compression tests while characterizing the phase constitution (using XRD), the microstructure (using SEM/BSE), and secondary mechanical properties (Vickers hardness and nanoindentation). Compare the engineering stress–strain curves, focusing on yield strength, ultimate strength, and fracture strain.
measurements: Compressive yield strength and fracture strain from stress–strain curves
Elastic modulus via nanoindentation and impulse-excitation measurements
Phase and microstructural analysis via XRD and SEM/BSE
Vickers hardness under a 200 g load for 5 s
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb15Mo2.5Ta40V40W2.5 alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in ductility (e.g., compressive fracture strain remains near that of the equimolar baseline of ~2%) or shows a dramatic loss in yield strength and/or modulus that is inconsistent with predictions, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
